deep.reconstruction:
Overview. This page is the second half (rows 41-60) of a 60-row table that begins on the previous page. It works out a Gaussian-integer analogue of Gauss's lemma for one numerical case: the biquadratic (quartic) character of m = 9+10i modulo the prime q = 15+4i, whose norm is N = 241. The page ends with the column totals.

The columns, in order:
(1) P runs over a 'quarter system' of residues mod q. These are the Gaussian integers whose image P/q lies in the open square (0,1/2)x(0,1/2), in coordinates relative to q. There are exactly (241-1)/4 = 60 of them, matching the 40+20 rows on the two pages.
(2) 'D pi' = P*conj(q) = P*(15-4i). Example: (5+2i)(15-4i) = 83+10i. Both coordinates lie in (0,120.5), which is the quarter-system condition again.
(3) '2 D pi m' = P*(15-4i)*(18+20i), where 2m = 18+20i. Example: (83+10i)(18+20i) = 1294+1840i.
(4) [2p] = floor of (column 3)/241, taken in each coordinate separately. This is floor(2mP/q). Example: 1294/241 = 5.37 and 1840/241 = 7.63, giving 5+7i.
(5) The nabla column is the exponent lambda. Put d = [2p] - 2[p], which is always one of 0, 1, 1+i, i. Gauss writes lambda = 0, 1, 2, 3 for these four cases respectively. d records which quarter of the unit square the fractional part of mP/q falls in.
(6) Dp = (column 3)/2 = mP(15-4i).
(7) [p] = floor(Dp/241) = floor(mP/q).

Why lambda gives the character (my gloss). The residue mP mod q lies in quarter lambda of the fundamental square. Multiplication by i rotates that square about its centre (1+i)q/2, which is fixed mod q. So mP ≡ i^lambda P' with P' again in the quarter system. Taking the product over all 60 values of P gives m^60 ≡ i^(sum of lambda) (mod q).

Totals. The nabla column sums to 59 on the previous page and 34 on this page, so 93 in all, which is the '93' at the foot. Since 93 ≡ 1 mod 4, the character [ (9+10i)/(15+4i) ]_4 = i.

Independent check (mine). Modulo q we have i ≡ 177 (equivalently -64), so 9+10i ≡ 92. Then 92^60 ≡ 177 ≡ i (mod 241), confirming the result.

The last two columns (+ and -). Each row carries a value in {0,1,2,3}. Empirically:
- The value is the same 0/1/2/3 code applied to [p] mod 2. That is, Re[p] and Im[p] taken mod 2, with (0,0)->0, (1,0)->1, (1,1)->2, (0,1)->3.
- The value goes in the + column when Re P + Im P is even (P divisible by 1+i) and in the - column when P is odd.
- On this page the + column sums to 16 and the - column to 13. With the previous page (31 and 33) the totals are 47 and 46, the figures written at the foot.
- 47 - 46 = +1 ≡ 93 (mod 4). This is a second, independent evaluation of the same exponent. The 'Nach Upsilon geordnet' table on the previous page re-sorts these signed values by P, reduces mod 4 row by row, and also gets +1.

Remark. 9+10i (norm 181) and 15+4i (norm 241) are both primes, so this is likely a test case for biquadratic reciprocity between two primes, or for a lemma-type proof of it.

I could not fully reconstruct the theoretical identity behind the signed second column. The rule given above is inferred from the numbers.
errors: No arithmetic errors found in the 20 rows on this page. Spot-checked rows: 5+2i, 6+5i, 7+2i, 6+3i and others, both the products and the floors.
Row 3 (P = 5+3i) has a 0 in the + column and possibly a stray or struck 0 in the - column. Since the value is 0 this does not affect the totals.
Row 17 (P = 7+2i): by the parity rule (7+2 is odd) its value 0 belongs in the - column, which is where it is written. Harmless either way.
Previous page, row P = 3+3i: Dp should be 183+867i (half of 366+1734i), not '193'. [p] = 3i is still correct.

Previous page, row P = 3+5i: the product is -90+2434i and Dp is -45+1217i, i.e. negative real parts. The floors -1+10i and -1+5i are consistent with the negative values, so the '+' signs are transcription errors or slips.

Previous page, 'Nach Upsilon' list: the entry for P = 2+3i reads -2, but the main table gives -3 ([p] = 3i gives code 3, and P is odd so the sign is -). Either a slip or a misreading. The row reduces to -1 mod 4 under either value, and the stated grand total +1 and the 47/46 totals are consistent with -3.

results.what: Numerical evaluation of the quartic character of 9+10i modulo the prime 15+4i (N = 241). Uses a quarter system of residues and the quadrant code given by [2x] - 2[x]. Result: sum of lambda = 93, so the character is i.
results.modern_name: Gauss's lemma for quartic (biquadratic) residues in Z[i], in Eisenstein-style floor-function form
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass material on biquadratic residues, Werke II/VIII); the floor-function/lattice formulation is often associated with Eisenstein (1844)

results.what: Second evaluation of the same exponent: signed sum of the quadrant code of floor(mP/q) mod 2, with sign by the parity of P. Gives 47 - 46 = 1 ≡ 93 (mod 4).
results.modern_name: A transformation of the quartic Gauss-lemma sum (Gaussian-integer analogue of the lattice-point step in Gauss's third proof / Eisenstein's proof)
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein-type lattice-point arguments (1844); exact identity unsure

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's work on biquadratic residues and an analogue of his lemma in Z[i] are known from the Nachlass. This page is a careful worked example. The signed second evaluation, which reduces floor(mP/q) mod 2 with signs by the parity of P, hints at a lattice-point transformation in the style of Eisenstein's proofs, but only numerically.
